row.basis: engraved names / seal
row.note: The commentary joins a name to a distinguishing mark; Exodus has Israel's names engraved on shoulder stones like a signet, memorializing who the bearer represents.

row.basis: the Name placed on a people
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies its bearer; here the priests put YHWH's name on Israel and YHWH blesses them, making the name a communal identity.

row.basis: covenant sign in flesh
row.note: The commentary's burned mark identifies its bearer; circumcision is explicitly a covenant sign in the flesh, marking Abraham's descendants as belonging to the covenant.

row.basis: blood as identifying sign
row.note: The commentary describes a mark that makes its bearer recognizable; blood on the houses is a sign that YHWH sees and that protects those inside.

row.basis: mark on foreheads
row.note: The commentary's brand makes a bearer distinguishable; Ezekiel orders a mark on the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations, identifying them within the city.

row.basis: the marked are spared
row.note: The commentary's identifying brand can be read as a mark of belonging; Ezekiel's executioners must spare everyone bearing the mark, giving it an explicit protective function.

row.basis: writing YHWH's name on a hand
row.note: The commentary says a name is an identifying sign; Isaiah pictures a person writing “I am YHWH's” on the hand and taking Israel's name, making affiliation bodily visible.

row.basis: sign on hand and between the eyes
row.note: The commentary's brand is a bodily sign; Deuteronomy makes God's words a sign on the hand and frontlets between the eyes, a visible and remembered mark of allegiance.

row.basis: Sabbath sign that makes God known
row.note: The commentary connects a distinguishing mark with knowing; Sabbath is explicitly a sign between YHWH and Israel “that you may know” who sanctifies them.

row.basis: prohibited bodily marks
row.note: The commentary treats a burned brand as a mark that identifies; Leviticus forbids incisions and tattoo marks on the body for the dead, adding a distinct Israelite boundary around bodily marking.

row.basis: the Lamb's and Father's names on foreheads
row.note: The commentary treats a mark as a sign that identifies its bearer; Revelation names the Lamb's followers by the names written on their foreheads.

row.basis: seal on servants' foreheads
row.note: The commentary's brand distinguishes a bearer; Revelation seals God's servants on the forehead before harm reaches the earth.

row.basis: the beast's mark on hand or forehead
row.note: The commentary's mark identifies whose a bearer is; Revelation gives the beast's followers a contrary mark on hand or forehead, signaling a rival allegiance.

row.basis: mark, name, and number control buying
row.note: The commentary links a mark to recognition; Revelation connects the beast's mark with its name or number and access to trade, showing identity enforced publicly.

row.basis: stigmata borne on the body
row.note: The commentary's wasm image is a visible bodily trace; Paul says he bears Jesus' marks on his body. Here the marks are scars of suffering, so the connection is bodily identification, not a claim of literal branding.

row.basis: seal, God's knowledge, and naming the Lord
row.note: The commentary joins sign, name, and knowing; this verse says God's seal declares “the Lord knows those who are his” and addresses everyone who names the Lord.

row.basis: the good name invoked over believers
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies the one named; James calls Jesus' name the good name invoked over the community, making the name a mark of affiliation.

row.basis: baptism into a name
row.note: The commentary says beginning under a name places an act beneath that identity; Jesus commissions baptism into the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, marking discipleship.

row.basis: sheep called individually by name
row.note: The commentary describes a rising shape becoming recognizable; the shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they recognize his voice, making naming a concrete act of recognition.

row.basis: tribal standards identify camps
row.note: The commentary calls the world and each species a distinguishing sign; Israel camps by its tribal standard, which marks each group within the larger people.

row.basis: YHWH named as a banner
row.note: The commentary brings a raised name together with a standard; Moses names the altar “YHWH is my banner,” explicitly joining divine name and battle sign.

row.basis: a sign whose child bears a revealing name
row.note: The commentary makes a name an elevated sign; Isaiah's promised sign is a child named Immanuel, “God with us,” whose name interprets the sign.

row.basis: the majestic name over earth and heavens
row.note: The commentary reads the opening Name as raised for recognition; the psalm calls YHWH's name majestic in all the earth and places glory above the heavens.

row.basis: the Name blessed forever
row.note: The commentary cites a name praised as exalted; this verse blesses YHWH's name from now and forever, giving the name an enduring liturgical praise.

row.basis: the Name high above nations
row.note: The commentary joins name and height; the psalm says YHWH is high above all nations and his glory above the heavens.

row.basis: the Name alone exalted over creation
row.note: The commentary makes every created kind a sign of its Lord; the psalm calls all creation to praise the name, which alone is exalted over earth and heaven.

row.basis: creatures as witnesses
row.note: The commentary says each created kind is itself a sign; Job tells the hearer to ask beasts, birds, and the earth, which teach what humans should recognize.

row.basis: creation points to its maker
row.note: The commentary reads the world as a mark by which its Lord is known; Job concludes that the hand of YHWH made these things.

row.basis: the creator calls stars by name
row.note: The commentary joins creation, distinction, and knowing; Isaiah says God brings out the starry host by number and calls each by name, with none missing.

row.basis: the heavens announce their maker
row.note: The commentary says the world is a sign that makes its Lord known; the heavens declare God's glory and the firmament announces his handiwork.

row.basis: created beauty reveals its maker
row.note: The commentary calls every created kind a sign; Wisdom says the greatness and beauty of created things let observers recognize their maker.

row.basis: creation makes the creator's qualities perceptible
row.note: The commentary reads the created world as a sign of its Lord; Romans says God's invisible attributes are understood through the things made.

row.basis: the divine name hallowed in prayer
row.note: The commentary opens with Allah's name and gives a spoken invocation; Jesus teaches prayer by asking that the Father's name be hallowed.

row.basis: every deed done in the Lord's name
row.note: The commentary says to begin an act in God's name is to place it under that recognized sign; Paul extends this to every word and deed done in Jesus' name.

row.basis: the name above every name
row.note: The commentary calls Allah the greatest name and develops the image of a name raised high; Paul says God gave Jesus the name above every name.

row.basis: glory due the Name and an offering
row.note: The commentary links the divine name with worship and placing work under that name; the psalm asks worshipers to ascribe glory due his name and bring an offering.

row.basis: proclaiming the Name and ascribing greatness
row.note: The commentary says Allah's name is the greatest and raised for recognition; Moses proclaims YHWH's name and calls the hearers to ascribe greatness to God.

row.basis: calling on the Lord's name
row.note: The commentary includes the invocation “O Allah, forgive me”; Acts promises salvation to everyone who calls on the Lord's name.

row.basis: an altar labeled “unknown god”
row.note: The commentary warns that a raised name can lack what it is supposed to identify; Paul takes an altar's label for an unknown god and announces the creator as the referent, while Luke preserves the Athenians' admission of ignorance.

row.basis: idols have no real existence
row.note: The commentary says humanly assigned deity names may be only names; Paul says an idol is nothing and there is one God, a close polemical counterpart.

row.basis: a deity is not a human-made image
row.note: The commentary says humanly assigned names can have nothing beneath them; Acts says the divine being is not like gold, silver, or stone shaped by human art and imagination.

row.basis: Adam and the naming of creatures
row.note: The commentary recalls Adam being taught names; Genesis has God bring the animals to Adam to see what he will call them, a shared naming scene.

row.basis: who teaches or gives the names
row.note: The commentary cites Qur'an 2:31, where God teaches Adam all the names; Genesis instead has God bring animals for Adam to name, shifting agency and the scope of the naming scene.

row.basis: Noah and the ark's boarding
row.note: The commentary cites Noah addressing those boarding the ark; Genesis has YHWH command Noah and his household to enter it, preserving the shared boarding scene but assigning the speech to God.

row.basis: the ark comes to rest
row.note: The commentary says Noah places the ark's sailing and mooring under God's name; Genesis reports that the ark came to rest on Ararat without naming that action as an invocation.

row.basis: smoke over the destroyed cities
row.note: The commentary cites Lot's overturned city as a sign for discerning readers; Genesis has Abraham look toward Sodom and see smoke rising like a furnace, a visible trace left by the same destruction.

row.basis: the Queen of Sheba hears Solomon's fame
row.note: The commentary's letter scene names Solomon and the Queen of Sheba; Kings says she came after hearing Solomon's fame concerning YHWH's name, linking the same queen and the divine name.

row.basis: the Queen blesses Solomon's God
row.note: The commentary's Sheba letter begins in Allah's name; after testing Solomon, the biblical queen blesses YHWH, his God, giving the shared encounter a spoken praise of the sender's deity.

row.basis: calling on the divine name
row.note: The commentary includes calling Allah by name; Genesis says people began to call on the name of YHWH, an early narrative use of invocation.

row.basis: a great name given by God
row.note: The commentary says a good name rises and spreads among people; God promises Abram that he will make his name great, making reputation a bestowed sign.

row.basis: a name made for oneself
row.note: The commentary contrasts the highest divine name with empty names assigned by humans; Babel's builders explicitly seek to make a name for themselves, a human project of self-exaltation.

row.basis: the divine name as memorial
row.note: The commentary treats a name as what makes its bearer known; Exodus gives YHWH's name as a memorial for all generations.

row.basis: the Name remembered at an altar
row.note: The commentary connects God's name with invocation and beginning an act under it; Exodus says YHWH will come and bless at every place where he causes his name to be remembered.

row.basis: the name must not be borne falsely
row.note: The commentary presents the name as a mark placed over an action; the command against bearing YHWH's name in vain gives that practice an ethical limit.

row.basis: an action begun in YHWH's name
row.note: The commentary says beginning work in God's name places the deed under that sign; David enters battle saying he comes against Goliath in the name of YHWH.

row.basis: YHWH's name proclaimed
row.note: The commentary presents Allah as the greatest name and as a name spoken in invocation; here YHWH descends and proclaims the divine name to Moses.

row.basis: the proclaimed name described as merciful
row.note: The opening formula names Allah with al-Rahman and al-Rahim; Exodus follows the proclamation of YHWH's name with “merciful and gracious,” connecting divine naming with mercy.

row.basis: name and compassion formula
row.note: The commentary's 1:1 includes the names al-Rahman and al-Rahim; Exodus places YHWH's name beside the description “merciful and gracious,” a close formula-level bridge.

row.basis: Joseph speaks to fellow prisoners
row.note: The commentary's Qur'an 12:40 places Joseph's religious speech among prison companions; in Genesis 40:8 he tells two inmates that interpretations belong to God. Genesis does not discuss their idols, so the shared prison speech makes the difference in subject clear.

row.basis: sailors invoke YHWH in danger at sea
row.note: The commentary has Noah invoke God's name over the ark's movement and rest; Jonah's sailors cry to YHWH during a life-threatening voyage, joining divine invocation to a vessel at sea.

row.basis: the Name as a refuge
row.note: The commentary says an act begun in God's name is placed under that sign; Proverbs says YHWH's name is a strong tower into which the righteous run, making the name protective.

row.basis: names recorded before YHWH
row.note: The commentary treats a name as what distinguishes and makes a bearer known; Malachi describes a book of remembrance written before YHWH for those who fear him and esteem his name.

row.basis: names written in heaven
row.note: The commentary makes a name an identifying mark; Jesus tells his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven, a written record of belonging.

row.basis: the Father's name made known
row.note: The commentary says a name lets its bearer be known; Jesus says he has manifested the Father's name to the disciples, connecting revelation of the name with recognition.

row.basis: letters written and sealed in a king's name
row.note: The commentary says a letter's opening name identifies its sender and authority; Jezebel writes in Ahab's name and seals the letters with his seal, showing the name and mark authorizing a document.

row.basis: a decree in the king's name, sealed
row.note: The commentary reads the basmala at the head of Solomon's letter as an authority marker; Esther's officials write a decree in the king's name and seal it with his ring.

row.basis: Matthew's reading of Isaiah's sign-name
row.note: Isaiah's sign child is named Immanuel; Matthew applies the name “God with us” to Jesus, making the name a Christian reading of the sign's referent.

row.basis: a name interprets the child's role
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies what is named; Matthew says Jesus is to be named for he will save his people, making the name a sign of his action.

row.basis: Exodus remembered as a sign
row.note: The commentary links a visible sign with knowing and recognition; Exodus says the deliverance from Egypt is to be a sign on the hand and a memorial between the eyes.

row.basis: righteous and wicked names remembered differently
row.note: The commentary says a good name circulates for good, not evil; Proverbs contrasts the blessed memory of the righteous with the rotting name of the wicked.

row.basis: a good name valued above good oil
row.note: The commentary says a good name rises among people; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than good oil, treating reputation as a lasting public distinction.

row.basis: Arabic ism / Hebrew shem
row.note: The Arabic word ism in 1:1 and Hebrew shem are Semitic cognates; Ecclesiastes uses shem for a good reputation, matching the commentary's account of a name circulating as honor. Its s-m-w and w-s-m source labels are not the basis for this comparison.

row.basis: Arabic ism / Aramaic shema
row.note: The Arabic word ism in 1:1 and Aramaic shema are cognates; Daniel blesses God's name forever, showing the cognate in a liturgical use of the divine name.

row.basis: Arabic Allah / Hebrew El
row.note: The commentary names Allah in 1:1; Arabic Allah and Hebrew El/Eloah are related Semitic divine terms, while Jacob names an altar El-Elohe-Israel. The terms are cognate, not identical titles.

row.basis: Arabic al-Rahman / Hebrew rahum
row.note: The 1:1 formula includes al-Rahman and al-Rahim; Exodus calls YHWH rahum, “merciful.” These forms share the Semitic R-Ḥ-M root, while the commentary's listed root labels do not establish that relationship.

row.basis: the crown of a good name
row.note: The commentary says a good name rises among people; Avot says the crown of a good name surpasses Torah, priesthood, and kingship, turning reputation into the highest social distinction.

row.basis: the Name as written and its liturgical substitute
row.note: The commentary emphasizes calling Allah and naming him; the Mishnah distinguishes pronouncing the divine Name as written in the Temple from using a substitute elsewhere, showing that recognition and utterance are context-bound.

row.basis: the congregation answers the divine Name
row.note: The commentary pairs God's name with invocation; in the High Priest's confession, the congregation responds with the blessing of God's glorious kingdom, making the Name part of communal liturgy.

row.basis: the mark on Ezekiel's foreheads interpreted as a letter
row.note: The commentary's brand is a sign read on a body; the Talmud debates what Ezekiel's tav-mark signifies, turning the mark into a letter whose reading distinguishes life from death.

row.basis: the attributes of mercy as a prayer order
row.note: The commentary gives an invocation asking Allah for forgiveness and names Allah with mercy epithets; this tradition reads Exodus 34's proclaimed attributes as a prayer pattern by which Israel seeks forgiveness.

row.basis: tribal banners as detailed identity signs
row.note: The commentary treats a standard as a distinguishing mark; the midrash elaborates the tribal banners by colors and stones, making the standards a visual code for each tribe.

row.basis: regard for a name that outlasts wealth
row.note: The commentary says a name spreads as a person's public honor; Sirach urges regard for one's name because it remains longer than great stores of gold.

row.basis: the Temple response blesses the Name
row.note: The commentary says Allah's name is called in prayer; this Mishnah preserves the Temple response “Blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever,” an explicit liturgical elevation of the Name.

row.basis: Cain's sign protects its bearer
row.note: The commentary's camel brand lets observers recognize its bearer; Genesis says God gives Cain a sign so that anyone finding him will not kill him, though it does not say the sign is a bodily brand.

row.basis: a changed name as a promise-sign
row.note: The commentary treats a name as an identifying sign; God changes Abram's name to Abraham because he will be father of many nations, so the name points to a promised identity.

row.basis: human self-naming at Babel
row.note: The commentary contrasts the highest divine name with names assigned by humans; Babel's builders seek to make their own name through a tower, a specific reversal of placing a deed under God's name.

row.basis: rainbow as covenant sign
row.note: The commentary defines an identifying trace; God sets the bow in the cloud as a sign of the covenant between God and earth, adding a visible sign that recalls a relation.

row.basis: tribal names borne over the heart
row.note: The commentary says a name makes its bearer known; the high priest carries Israel's names over his heart as a memorial before YHWH, so the names identify the people in worship.

row.basis: engraved Name on the high priest's forehead
row.note: The commentary joins a distinguishing sign with a name; Aaron wears a gold plate engraved “Holy to YHWH” on his forehead, a literal inscribed name-mark.

row.basis: a visible fringe prompts recognition
row.note: The commentary says reading a mark means seeing a trace; Israelites are to see the fringes, remember the commandments, and do them, making a worn sign a prompt to recognize and obey.

row.basis: names written on tribal staffs
row.note: The commentary links names with identifying marks; the tribal leaders' names are written on their staffs, and Aaron's name is written on Levi's staff.

row.basis: a blossoming staff identifies God's choice
row.note: The commentary says a mark distinguishes one bearer from others; the staff that blossoms identifies the person YHWH chooses and is to end the people's complaints.

row.basis: “Holy to YHWH” on horse bells
row.note: The commentary's brand marks a bearer so it can be recognized; Zechariah says even horses' bells will bear an inscription of holiness to YHWH, extending the Name-mark to animal equipment.

row.basis: the prophet and his children as signs
row.note: The commentary calls each created kind a sign; Isaiah says he and the children YHWH gave him are signs and portents in Israel, making human lives and names part of the message.

row.basis: called by name and claimed as God's own
row.note: The commentary says a name identifies its bearer; YHWH says he has called Israel by name and that Israel is his, directly joining recognition with belonging.

row.basis: Moses known by name
row.note: The commentary defines a name as what makes a being known; YHWH tells Moses, “I know you by name,” giving that definition a direct biblical use.

row.basis: knowing God's name brings protection
row.note: The commentary says a name is a mark by which its bearer is known; God promises deliverance to the one who knows his name, linking recognition with protection.

row.basis: pardon requested for the sake of God's name
row.note: The commentary gives the invocation “O Allah, forgive me”; the psalmist asks YHWH to pardon his iniquity for the sake of YHWH's name. This is Hebrew WLC numbering; the petition is commonly numbered Psalm 25:11 in English.

row.basis: service and oath in the divine name
row.note: The commentary joins the name with worship and calling; Deuteronomy commands Israel to fear and serve YHWH and swear by his name.

row.basis: call on the Name and tell its deeds among nations
row.note: The commentary says a good name circulates among people; this hymn joins calling on YHWH's name with making his deeds known among the peoples.

row.basis: creation praises the Name because it was created
row.note: The commentary joins the divine name to all created kinds as signs; the psalm says creation praises YHWH's name because he commanded and it was created.

row.basis: people fail to read creation's sign
row.note: The commentary says created things make their Lord knowable; Wisdom says some observe the works but fail to recognize their maker, a specific failure to read the sign.

row.basis: stars answer when their maker calls
row.note: The commentary says each created kind is a sign and names make things recognizable; Baruch pictures stars answering their maker's call and shining for him, giving creation a responsive voice.

row.basis: God as maker and Lord of the whole world
row.note: The commentary reads al-ʿālamīn as the created realm belonging to its Lord; Paul identifies the unknown God as maker of the world and Lord of heaven and earth.

row.basis: weather and harvest as witness
row.note: The commentary says creation bears signs of its Lord; Paul says God did not leave himself without witness, giving rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness.

row.basis: many “so-called” gods, but one God
row.note: The commentary says gods named by people may be only names; Paul distinguishes so-called gods from the one God acknowledged by believers.

row.basis: no other saving name
row.note: The commentary calls Allah the greatest name and asks whether any equal deserves God's name; Peter says no other name under heaven is given by which people must be saved.

row.basis: every knee bows at Jesus' name
row.note: The commentary joins the highest name with worship; Paul says every knee bows at the name of Jesus, showing what exaltation of the Name entails.

row.basis: every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord
row.note: The commentary connects divine naming with worship and calling; Paul adds that every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord, the verbal response to the name's exaltation.

row.basis: the Name preserves the disciples
row.note: The commentary treats a name as the mark that identifies a bearer; Jesus asks the Father to keep the disciples in the Father's name, giving the name a protective and communal role.

row.basis: forgiveness proclaimed in Jesus' name to all nations
row.note: The commentary includes calling Allah for forgiveness and names Allah with mercy; Jesus commissions repentance and forgiveness to be proclaimed in his name to all nations.

row.basis: all who call on YHWH's name are saved
row.note: The commentary includes invocation of Allah's name; Joel promises deliverance to everyone who calls on YHWH's name. Hebrew WLC numbering places this at Joel 3:5, often Joel 2:32 in English.

row.basis: no one is like YHWH
row.note: The commentary explains “semiyy” as an equal worthy of God's name; the song asks who among the gods is like YHWH, giving a direct biblical formulation of divine incomparability.

row.basis: none like YHWH, whose name is great
row.note: The commentary says Allah is the greatest name and has no equal namesake; Jeremiah says none is like YHWH and that his name is great in might.

row.basis: signs and wonders make a name
row.note: The commentary joins the name as a sign with creation as signs of the Lord; Jeremiah says God performed signs and wonders and made a name for himself, explicitly bringing the two images together.

row.basis: the people bear YHWH's called name before nations
row.note: The commentary treats a name as a sign identifying its bearer; the nations see that YHWH's name is called over Israel and fear them.

row.basis: midrash on Adam naming the animals
row.note: The commentary recalls Adam receiving names; the midrash expands Genesis's naming scene by treating Adam's naming of the creatures as an act of discernment, making the name's relation to what is named explicit.

row.basis: the divine name as a promise of presence
row.note: The commentary says a name is more than an arbitrary label and is spoken in invocation; this midrash reads God's answer to Moses as a pledge of presence with Israel in its affliction.

row.basis: mercy includes accountability
row.note: The commentary pairs God's name with mercy; the continuation says YHWH forgives iniquity yet does not simply clear guilt, preserving the judgment side of the name-and-mercy formula.

row.basis: Arabic al-ʿālamīn / Syriac ʿālmā
row.note: The Qur'anic word al-ʿālamīn and Syriac ʿālmā (“world”) appear to be related forms, though the commentary's ʿ-l-m labels do not prove cognacy. The Peshitta says the world was made through the Word yet did not know him, a specific counterpoint to the commentary's world as a sign by which its Lord is known.

row.basis: visible religious signs used for public honor
row.note: The commentary says a sign makes a bearer recognizable and notes that a good name can spread among people; Jesus criticizes enlarging phylacteries to be seen by others, showing how a visible religious mark can become a bid for reputation.

row.basis: a public name written on the forehead
row.note: The commentary treats a mark or name as a readable identity; Revelation places the name “Babylon the Great” on the woman's forehead, using inscription to expose a rival allegiance.

row.basis: a title written on robe and thigh
row.note: The commentary develops names as visible marks of identity; the rider's garment bears “King of kings and Lord of lords,” a public inscription of authority.

row.basis: a written name no one knows
row.note: The commentary says a name makes its bearer recognizable; Revelation's rider bears a written name known only to himself, preserving a counter-reading in which the sign marks identity without making it public.

row.basis: the divine wrestler's name withheld
row.note: The commentary defines a name as what lets one know its bearer; Jacob asks the divine wrestler's name but receives the reply “Why do you ask my name?”, setting a limit on that knowledge.

row.basis: a place named after seeing God
row.note: The commentary says a name is a sign by which a reality is recognized; Jacob names the place Peniel after seeing God face to face, turning an encounter into a place-name.
